source.title: Recipes for Building an Open-Domain Chatbot
source.authors: Stephen Roller; Emily Dinan; Naman Goyal; Da Ju; Mary Williamson; Yinhan Liu; Jing Xu; Myle Ott; Kurt Shuster; Eric Michael Smith; Y-Lan Boureau; J. Weston

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures validation perplexity for differently sized generative models and reports a human-evaluation comparison between two sizes. It does not fit scaling laws or reproduce the original scaling-law procedure.
record.gate_note: The relevant outcomes are the pretraining validation perplexities in Table 2 and the direct 2.7B-versus-9.4B engagingness comparison in Section 10.3. The paper cites other work on scaling; those cited results are not recorded as rows. It does not report a power-law fit or a compute-optimal allocation.
record.test_reason: This is a chatbot-recipe paper, not a scaling-law study. Its own results bear on V6 in a new setting: human evaluations of dialogue quality across 90M, 2.7B and 9.4B generative models are set against their pretraining perplexity. For V1 it gives only two directly comparable perplexity points (2.7B and 9.4B), which cannot show a power law over orders of magnitude. No fits, extrapolation, compute allocation or shape sweep are reported.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors find the 2.7B model gives large gains over the 90M model, but the 9.4B model has no clear win over the 2.7B model in human evaluations despite lower perplexity. They say the link between perplexity and human judgments is not straightforward. They argue that training data (BST fine-tuning) and decoding choices matter beyond scale and perplexity.
record.recipe_differences: The paper reports perplexities and dialogue evaluations for chatbot models of several sizes; it does not perform the original scaling-law fitting procedure or systematically vary training compute and data.
record.method_sensitivity: Perplexity comparisons depend on vocabulary: the 90M model's dictionary differs from those of the larger models. Human-evaluation outcomes also vary with decoding and training choices discussed in the paper.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 5: the 9.4B model reaches a given validation perplexity in fewer SGD steps than the 2.7B model. The authors say this is consistent with Kaplan et al. (2020).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger language models are more sample-efficient, reaching a given loss in fewer steps or tokens.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference of the European Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: Only the 2.7B and 9.4B pretraining perplexities are directly comparable; the 90M model uses a different dictionary. The paper does not fit scaling exponents, report uncertainty for the perplexity values, or test a compute-optimal split. The 2.7B model had not converged when training stopped.
record.rows_left_out: Table 3 reports perplexities after fine-tuning on dialogue tasks, but does not test whether those values follow a power law; those results are not included as evidence for the listed versions. Figure 5's training curves repeat the validation-perplexity trend without exact curve values in the text.

untested.parts: Power-law form, a range of several orders of magnitude, and variation of tokens or compute. Only two comparable sizes are reported.
Entirely untested. The two models differ in depth and width only as a consequence of their size.
No power-law fit for fine-tuning. Table 3 gives only two comparable fine-tuned sizes (8.98 vs 8.59 average PPL).
Standard downstream benchmarks and any fitted relation between loss and task score are untested. Only pairwise human dialogue judgments at three sizes are available.

missing.what: 90M vs 2.7B BST Generative engagingness: 43 vs 57 in self-chat (not significant).
Win rates against Meena by model size. Engagingness: 90M 61%, 2.7B 75%, 9.4B 67%. Humanness: 90M 59%, 2.7B 65%, 9.4B 66%.
Fine-tuned validation perplexity on the BST tasks, 2.7B vs 9.4B (average 8.98 vs 8.59), and pre-trained 2.7B vs 9.4B on the same tasks (13.71 vs 12.95).

record.verdict_notes: The study gives weak evidence on scaling: three sizes, of which only two have comparable perplexities, and pairwise human judgments with about 100 conversations per model. The 2.7B model had not converged when training stopped. The V6 challenge rests on a 56/44 split whose significance is not reported, and it concerns human dialogue preference rather than benchmark accuracy.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not fit or test a power law, establish behavior over several orders of magnitude, vary training-token count or compute systematically, or show that other quantities are not bottlenecks.
The paper reports an engagingness comparison for two model sizes, but does not test predictability across a range of downstream tasks or assess a predictive relation to pretraining loss.

rows.subject: 90M generative Transformer
rows.operation_detail: Compared validation perplexity across generative Transformer model sizes.
rows.note: The paper says this model uses a different dictionary from the 2.7B and 9.4B models, so their perplexities are not directly comparable.
rows.check: The 90M model uses a different dictionary (55K vs 8K) and a less-filtered corpus variant (footnote 4). It also trained for 2.86M steps, and its value is cited from Shuster et al. (2019). It cannot enter a size trend and should not carry a V1 label.

rows.subject: 2.7B generative Transformer
rows.operation_detail: Compared validation perplexity across generative Transformer model sizes.

conditions.value: 9.4B model; 90M model is not directly comparable because its dictionary differs

rows.note: The 2.7B model's perplexity is higher than the 9.4B model's on the shared dictionary.
rows.check: r2 and r3 are one two-point comparison (13.3 vs 12.2 PPL), so they should be merged. Lower perplexity at 9.4B agrees with V1 in direction, but two sizes about 3.5x apart cannot show a power law over orders of magnitude. The 2.7B model had not converged, though both models trained for 200K steps at about 500k tokens per batch.

rows.subject: 9.4B generative Transformer
rows.operation_detail: Compared validation perplexity across generative Transformer model sizes.
rows.note: The paper says the 2.7B and 9.4B perplexities are directly comparable; the larger model has lower perplexity.
rows.check: Duplicate of r2 with baseline and value swapped; same limitation.

rows.subject: BST Generative 2.7B
rows.operation_detail: Direct pairwise ACUTE-Eval comparison of engagingness against the 9.4B model.
rows.note: The authors report this comparison alongside the 9.4B model's lower perplexity.
rows.check: The 2.7B model beat the 9.4B model 56% to 44% on engagingness in a direct ACUTE-Eval, with no significance reported. The reversal is small and possibly non-significant. Both models had BST fine-tuning and the same decoding.

source_check.locator_found: Section 10.3, paragraph following Figure 15: direct 2.7B versus 9.4B engagingness evaluation.

relationships.reason: The 9.4B model has lower perplexity (12.2 vs 13.3) but loses 44% to 56% in a direct comparison. It also scores 67% vs 75% for the 2.7B model against Meena (r4; Figure 15 from text).
relationships.display_finding: The 9.4B model reduced perplexity from 13.3 to 12.2 but lost directly 44% to 56%, and scored 67% against Meena versus 75% for 2.7B.

source_check.label: challenges
source_check.reason: Section 10.3 reports a reversed size trend: the smaller model wins 56% directly and scores 75% against Meena versus 67% for 9.4B. Direct-comparison significance is not reported. The cited perplexities are pretraining measurements.

relationships.reason: The larger model wins in self-chat (57 vs 43, not significant) and against Meena (75% vs 61%). The verdict is based on the text, since no row records this (see missing).
relationships.display_finding: The larger model's self-chat advantage was statistically insignificant at 57% versus 43%, while engagingness wins against Meena increased from 61% to 75%.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.reason: Evidence differs by evaluation setting: Figure 10 explicitly calls the direct 57% versus 43% self-chat result nonsignificant, which the state rules classify as absent. Figure 15 shows a favorable indirect trend against Meena, 75% versus 61%. The combined condition needs qualification.

relationships.condition: BST Generative 2.7B vs 9.4B, humanness against Meena
relationships.reason: The two sizes score almost the same (66% for 9.4B vs 65% for 2.7B), so the perplexity gain barely transfers on this metric. The verdict is based on Figure 16 in the text; no row records it.
relationships.display_finding: Humanness scores are nearly identical at 66% for 9.4B and 65% for 2.7B despite the perplexity improvement.

tranche.reason: Reports results bearing on downstream predictability in a new setting: open-domain dialogue evaluated by human engagingness and humanness judgments.

source_check.notes: The authors' conclusion is accurately paraphrased. Separate pretraining perplexity measurements from BST-fine-tuned evaluations; neither the direct 2.7B–9.4B result nor the one-point humanness difference establishes statistical significance.

statements.correction: Table 2: pretraining Reddit-validation perplexity, 9.4B = 12.2; 2.7B = 13.3. Section 10.3: BST-fine-tuned 2.7B wins 56% against 9.4B; complementary preference = 44%; significance not reported.
statements.problem: The perplexities 12.2 and 13.3 describe pretraining checkpoints evaluated on Reddit, rather than the BST-fine-tuned checkpoints named in the statement. The engagingness comparison is correct.
